subject: SLO discovery — Arbor Health: latency vs input ceiling and streaming requirements
snippet: Post-call recap focused on context window ceilings, end-to-end latency targets, streaming behavior, and a proposed canary for concurrency/throughput.

From: Ellen Park <ellen.park@arborhealth.com>

Cc: aditya_rao@redwood.ai

Subject: SLO discovery — Arbor Health: latency vs input ceiling and streaming requirements

Thanks again for the demo earlier. Quick recap from our side and a few clarifying questions so we can scope the pilot: 

Summary of what we need
- Primary use: clinical summarization for multi-document patient notes (avg input ~6 documents, ~12k tokens pre-merge).
- Output: compressed summary, typically 150-400 tokens depending on the template.
- Hard requirement: streaming/partial output so UI can show incremental summary progress for clinicians.
- Target SLO: perceived UI latency (first token) <= 350ms on p95 in our US region; full summary within 2s preferred but not strict for longer inputs.
- Throughput: 50 concurrent clinician sessions during peak; expected steady-state concurrent 15.

Questions we need answered
1) Given ~12k token input, what's realistic for max context you can support server-side vs chunking/fallthrough?
2) For streaming, how does your runtime impact first-token latency vs total generation time (esp. with KV cache warm/unwarm)?
3) If we quantize and use a model variant, what latency improvements vs potential quality regressions should we expect?

Attached a spreadsheet with a few example notes and a sample UI sketch (arbor_perf_reqs.xlsx).

Next steps
- Can we get a proposed SLO/arch note back from Redwood summarizing tradeoffs and a recommended pilot config?
- Schedule a follow-up deep-dive (30–45m) with your performance team.

Thanks,
Ellen Park
Senior PM, Clinical AI
Arbor Health

Ellen — thanks for the clear notes and the sample data; very helpful. High-level responses below and a proposed pilot approach.

Quick answers to your numbered questions
1) Max context: hosting a single ~12k token input in one shot is possible but will push memory and batch-sizing. We typically recommend chunk+KV stitching for inputs > ~8k tokens to avoid long tail latency spikes. Chunking strategy keeps first-token latency low for streaming because you can start generating as soon as the first chunk is ingested.

2) Streaming and first-token latency: the runtime prioritizes reducing first-byte latency by warming KV and using small initial batches for interactive sessions. Typical first-token p95 for a streaming call with a warm KV and 2k input is ~120–180ms; for much larger inputs the first-token is dominated by input pre-processing and initial attention compilation if kernels need to be selected. We can instrument per-stage timing in the pilot so you see client->first-token and token-per-ms profiles.

3) Quantization: moving to 4-bit quantized weights commonly yields 1.6–2.2x throughput improvement and ~10–15% latency reduction on generation-heavy paths. Quality regression depends on model and evaluation prompts; for summarization templates we often see negligible difference but we’ll include A/B evals in the pilot.

Proposed pilot configuration (what we'd run for a 4-week quick qualification)
- Ingress: chunk inputs to ~4k token windows, stitch with KV caching to keep context semantics.
- Model: open-model variant in FP16 for baseline; a quantized 4-bit variant for a cost/latency run.
- SLO targets to validate: first-token p95 <= 300ms (warm); end-to-end p95 for 300–500 token outputs <= 1.2s for chunked flows.
- Concurrency plan: reserve a canary pool sized for 25 concurrent sessions, and run progressive ramp to 50 concurrent to measure queuing/backpressure behavior.
- Observability: per-request traces, token-timing breakdown, and a delta-quality eval on your prompt set.

We can sketch the exact autoscaling/queueing thresholds once we review the examples you attached. I propose a 30-minute handoff call with our perf engineer (Laura) tomorrow or Wed — which day works for your team?

Attachments: p95_latency_playbook.pdf (playbook excerpt)

— Karthik
Karthik Iyer
Enterprise Solutions, Redwood Inference

Ellen — adding a few concrete numbers and a short runbook for the pilot so you can validate against your UI expectations.

Pilot runbook highlights
- Ingest path: parallel upload of note chunks while we build KV cache; aim to accept first chunk in <80ms (network permitting).
- KV warming: for repeated clinician sessions we keep a warm pool for the last N patients (configurable); cold-start first-token delta typically +80–250ms depending on model size and kernel compile cache hit.
- Estimated latency matrix (ballpark; we'll measure exacts in pilot):
  * Small input (<=2k tokens), warm KV: first-token p95 110–150ms; token rate ~50–80 tokens/s (fast gen profile).
  * Medium input (2k–6k), warm KV: first-token p95 140–220ms; end-to-end 200–800ms for 150–400 token outputs.
  * Large input (>6k, chunked): first-token p95 180–320ms (depends on ingest parallelism); full summary p95 often 800ms–2.2s for 150–400 token outputs depending on chunk count.

Concurrency/throughput guidance
- With continuous batching off (interactive mode) and reserved canary pool, expect linear scaling to ~100 concurrent sessions on a modest dedicated GPU fleet (Nvidia H100-class equivalent) when using quantized variants; FP16 will require more capacity for the same concurrency.
- We recommend setting soft concurrency limit at 60 and autoscale/burst to 100 for peak tests to observe queuing effects.

Fallback and quality checks
- If p95 first-token breaches 400ms consistently, fallback to: increase chunk parallelism, drop to a narrower model variant for the initial token with synchronous rerank, or serve first-token from a distilled prefix model while the full model completes in background.

Next steps and actions assigned
- Redwood: create pilot config + cost estimate (Karthik) — delivery by EOD Wed 5/12.
- Redwood: schedule a perf handoff meeting (30m) — I can take Wed 9–11am PT or Thu 1–3pm PT.
- Arbor: confirm preferred follow-up time and share 3–5 representative notes in the spreadsheet that are most critical for fidelity.
